title: The Billable Hour Is Cracking: The Margin Question Every IT and Management Consultancy Now Faces
excerpt: AI is quietly compressing the hours behind every consulting engagement while overheads stay fixed. The consultancies protecting margin are the ones repricing before the market forces it on them.
content:
A management consultant we spoke with recently finished a scoping report in under half a day. The same report, eighteen months ago, would have taken her two and a half days of research, drafting and formatting. She billed the client the same day rate as always and felt a small twinge of guilt about it, even though the client was thrilled with the turnaround.

That twinge is becoming a familiar feeling across IT and management consulting firms on the East Coast. AI tools are now doing the first draft of the report, the initial code scaffold, the data pull, the slide deck skeleton. The work still gets reviewed, refined and delivered by a human, but the raw hours behind it are shrinking. Meanwhile the salaries, the leases, the software licences and the partner draw haven't shrunk at all.

This isn't really an AI story. It's a pricing and margin story that AI has simply forced into the open earlier than most consultancies expected to face it.

The Hours Are Shrinking, the Overheads Are Not

Most consulting practices were built on a simple assumption: a given engagement takes roughly this many hours, priced at roughly this rate, delivering roughly this margin. That assumption sat quietly underneath everything, from how many consultants get hired to what a partner expects to draw each quarter.

When the hours behind an engagement compress but the fee structure doesn't move, the maths underneath the business changes even though nothing on the invoice looks different. A senior consultant can post a perfectly healthy utilisation number on paper, hours charged against hours available, while the actual value delivered per billable hour has shifted underneath them. The scoreboard still reads well. The business behind it is quietly changing shape.

Utilisation Was Never the Full Story

Utilisation tells you how busy people are. It has never told you whether that busyness is turning into profit. Realisation, the rate at which billed hours actually convert into collected revenue at the intended price, is the number that matters more, and it's the one AI-driven speed is putting pressure on first.

The pattern we typically see across owner-led consultancies is that revenue holds steady even as delivery gets faster, because the fee model hasn't caught up with the new delivery reality. That gap between speed and price is where margin quietly leaks. A workforce capacity and utilisation review is usually the fastest way to see exactly where that gap sits, engagement by engagement, before it shows up as a soft quarter.

The Pricing Model That Actually Matches Delivery Today

Clients were never really paying for hours. They were paying for a solved problem, a working system, a decision they felt confident making. Hourly billing was simply the easiest way to package that value when delivery time was the main constraint. Once AI removes some of that constraint, hourly billing starts working against the firms that rely on it, because the fee shrinks in step with the hours even though the client's problem is solved just as completely.

Reframing the client conversation

Firms that reprice around scope, outcome or a fixed project fee, rather than time logged, tend to hold their margin through this shift rather than watch it erode engagement by engagement. That's a deliberate, structured exercise rather than a New Year's resolution to charge more. A proper pricing reset looks at customer profitability and competitor positioning together, so the new fee structure is defensible rather than guessed at.

What to Measure Instead of Hours

Hours charged is an activity metric. Margin per engagement, revenue per consultant and contribution after the cost of the AI tools themselves are the numbers that actually describe whether the business is getting healthier or just faster. Firms that switch their monthly reporting to track these, rather than utilisation alone, tend to spot the pricing gap months before it shows up in a thin quarter.

None of this is a reason to slow down on adopting AI tools. It's a reason to make sure the commercial model underneath the practice keeps pace with how quickly the work itself is changing. That's usually the point where an outside fractional CFO perspective earns its keep, not to tell a partner how to run client work, but to keep the numbers honest while the delivery model shifts under everyone's feet. If you're weighing up whether that kind of support fits where your practice is at, our guide to what a fractional CFO actually does is a reasonable place to start.

faqs.q: How is AI affecting profit margins for IT and management consulting firms in Australia?
faqs.a: AI tools are compressing the hours needed to deliver research, drafting and technical scaffolding, while fixed costs like salaries and leases stay the same. For firms still billing by the hour, faster delivery can mean a smaller invoice for the same solved problem, which quietly erodes margin unless the pricing model is adjusted to match.

faqs.q: What is the difference between utilisation and realisation in a consulting business?
faqs.a: Utilisation measures how many available hours a consultant actually charges to clients. Realisation measures how much of that billed time is actually collected at the intended rate. A practice can show strong utilisation while realisation quietly slips, which is usually the earlier warning sign that pricing has fallen behind delivery reality.

faqs.q: Should an IT consultancy move from hourly billing to fixed fee pricing?
faqs.a: For many engagements, yes, particularly where AI tools have shortened delivery time without reducing the value of the outcome. A considered pricing reset that looks at customer profitability and competitor positioning tends to produce a more defensible fee structure than an ad hoc switch to fixed pricing.

faqs.q: How do I know if my consulting firm's pricing model is outdated?
faqs.a: The clearest signal is delivery speed increasing while margin per engagement stays flat or falls. If your team is finishing work faster than eighteen months ago but the invoice size hasn't changed, the fee structure is still tied to hours that no longer reflect how the work actually gets done.

faqs.q: What financial metrics matter most for a management consultancy right now?
faqs.a: Margin per engagement, revenue per consultant and contribution after the cost of AI tooling tell a more accurate story than utilisation alone. Tracking these monthly, rather than relying on hours charged, tends to surface a pricing gap several months before it appears as a soft quarter.

faqs.q: When should a growing consultancy bring in a fractional CFO?
faqs.a: Usually once delivery models, pricing or headcount are changing faster than the existing reporting can explain clearly. A fractional CFO brings outside financial structure to keep those numbers honest while the commercial model catches up with how the work is actually being delivered.

faqs.q: Does adopting AI tools mean a consultancy should cut its fees?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. The client is still paying for a solved problem, not for hours logged, so the case for cutting fees is weaker than it first appears. The more durable move is repricing around scope and outcome so the fee reflects the value delivered rather than shrinking in step with the time it took.
